http://mobileidworld.com/tele2-sets-2027.text: Estonian Mobile-ID users with older Tele2 SIM cards will need replacements before May 20, 2027, as the carrier updates the hardware behind its phone-based authentication and digital-signature service. Tele2 says affected customers must complete the switch by May 19 to keep using Mobile-ID without interruption. The carrier is replacing the cards to meet security requirements associated with the European Union’s eIDAS 2.0 framework. Customers whose cards need to be changed will receive a personalized notice by email, text message, or through Tele2’s self-service portal, and can also identify the updated cards by their new visual design. Mobile-ID stores a government-backed identity credential on the user’s SIM . A user enters separate PINs on the phone to authenticate to an online service or create a legally binding digital signature, giving the handset many of the same electronic identity functions as Estonia’s physical ID card without requiring a card reader. The replacement is free for existing Tele2 Mobile-ID users and can be ordered through the carrier’s self-service portal or obtained at a Tele2 store. Because the certificates on an older SIM cannot be transferred to the replacement card, customers must establish a new Mobile-ID service and receive new certificates after making the switch. Digital signatures created with the previous card will remain valid. Customers who do not replace an affected SIM by the deadline will still be able to make calls, send messages, and use mobile data. The change applies specifically to Mobile-ID functions, including online sign-in and digital signing; users would otherwise need to authenticate with an alternative such as Smart-ID or an ID card. The migration comes as Estonia continues updating the identity infrastructure supporting its mobile-first public services. The country recently began issuing new electronic identity cards with remotely updatable security software , while Mobile-ID and Smart-ID remain widely used routes into government, banking, and private-sector services. Photograph: Mark Edward Harris/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Ukraine Russia strikes Ukraine intelligence HQ in ‘major escalation’ Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has told SBU to deliver ‘appropriate, tangible response’ to Kyiv strike Amy Hawkins in Kyiv Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.37 EDT First published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 11.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The head office of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence agency has been hit in a Russian drone attack, sending plumes of black smoke rising into the air in the heart of Kyiv. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he had instructed the SBU to deliver an “appropriate, tangible response” to the strike, while the foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, described it as a “major escalation”. The streets around the SBU headquarters were cordoned off shortly after Friday’s attack, with armed officers patrolling the area. Numerous ambulances and emergency services vehicles were stationed around the site, which is close to St Sophia Cathedral, a Unesco world heritage site. “Unfortunately, a Russian drone hit the central building of the SBU on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv, opposite the St Sophia Cathedral,” Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram. “The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building.” Kyiv has been under a barrage of daily drone and missile attacks from Russia for over a week. Zelenskyy on Friday called for Russia to halt its attacks during a visit of US negotiators, Steve Witkoff ‌and Jared Kushner, to the city on Sunday and said Ukraine would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace while they were in Moscow. Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors which can shoot down incoming threats. Many of the recent Russian strikes have been by new-model jet-powered drones which can reach speeds of 250mph, making them hard to intercept. It is rare for government buildings in central Kyiv to be reached by Russian strikes, especially in broad daylight. The explosion from the hit on the SBU building could be heard from several blocks away. The incident is likely to intensify the escalating attacks that Moscow and Kyiv have been launching at each other in recent weeks in efforts to destroy each other’s resilience and morale. It will also raise questions about Kyiv’s ability to defend its key infrastructure against Russia. Sybiha said the attack was “a major escalation that demands resolute responses” and called on international partners to “unequivocally condemn these actions and step up pressure on the Putin regime”. At least nine people were injured in Friday’s strike, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. Stanislav Zavertailo, the co-owner of the nearby Zavertailo cafe, said one of his customers was injured in the strike, which sent shockwaves through his premises, shattering all the windows. “It’s a normal cafe,” he said. The customer was “eating one of our famous poppy seed rolls” when the attack occurred, he added. Staff and customers rushed into an underground shelter after the strike, fearing a double-tap attack, a tactic which Russia has employed, in which a second drone is sent in soon after the first, hitting emergency service workers. An hour later, there had been no second strike, but Zavertailo said he did not feel at ease. “We are all waiting for another attack,” he said. The SBU is responsible for coordinating complex operations against Russia, including last year’s Operation Spiderweb which destroyed aircraft worth billions of pounds inside Russia. Friday’s hit was “awful” said a Zavertailo cafe employee who had recently emerged from the underground shelter. As “a person who lives in Ukraine for all this time, it’s just hard”. The strike came two days before Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were expected to visit Kyiv for the first time. US-led diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s four-and-a-half-year invasion have stalled in recent months as the US has shifted its focus towards the war with Iran. https://www.dw.com/en/trump-defends-russ.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OODy Trump (right) repeated his claim that Ukraine was targeting Russian refineries to hurt Republicans ahead of the US midterm election [FILE: September 22, 2026] Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement US President Donald Trump on Sunday defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, accusing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. "My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Zelenskyy doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," he added. Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving broad new sanctions mandated by legislation named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine's defense. He has also temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing supplies to flow into global markets in a bid to lower fuel prices ahead of US midterm elections on November 3. Trump links Russia sanctions waiver to fuel prices ahead of midterms Opinion polls suggest that Republicans could face significant losses in the election, as voters voice growing frustration over fuel prices that have surged since the Iran war began in late February. Most economists believe the suspension of congressionally approved sanctions on Russia and the diesel deal with the Kremlin will do little to lower US fuel prices. Trump also repeated his claim that Ukraine was targeting Russian refineries to hurt Republicans ahead of the midterm election. How Trump is helping Putin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The move drew a sharp response from Kyiv and its allies, further straining relations between Trump and Zelenskyy. Zelenskyy warns Ukraine cannot prevail if US backs Russia Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Sunday that Ukraine would lose its defensive battle against Russia if the United States switched sides and supported Moscow. "If the United States will take the side of Russia, of course we will not prevail," Zelenskyy told NBC's 'Meet the Press' calling a withdrawal of US support "a historic mistake and big tragedy." He said Washington had resumed sharing intelligence after it was "blocked for some period of time," adding that Ukraine had missed critical intelligence on ballistic missile attacks for three days. Zelenskyy also criticized US restrictions affecting Ukraine's war effort, saying, "We are strategic partners," but "we cannot applaud when someone turns against Ukraine." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended Trump's suspension of new sanctions on Russia, saying Trump wanted to assess their impact on the global and US economies. Zelenskyy speaks to US envoys as Trump renews criticism Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke to US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as Russia and Ukraine attacked each other's energy infrastructure, leaving thousands without power in Ukraine and setting an oil refinery ablaze near Saint Petersburg. After the talks, Zelenskyy said "a lot depends" on the US position, adding that "this war must be brought to an end." Ukraine was ready to work "constructively" and "honestly," he said, calling for the same approach from its European and US partners. Zelenskyy said he also discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defense systems as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles. A US-led push to end the war has yet to yield a breakthrough, with Trump expressing frustration at both Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Kyiv hit by Russian air strike as Ukraine targets Saint Petersburg Zelenskyy accused Moscow of violating Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warned Russia planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter. Russian strikes left "tens of thousands" without power, he said, while Ukrainian officials reported three deaths. A Russian air strike damaged a subway station on the left bank of Kyiv on Sunday, killing a 21-year-old woman and injuring three others, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Monday. A medical facility and a non-residential building were also damaged. Ukraine launched drones at Putin's hometown of Saint Petersburg late Sunday, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said. (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia) Read more Gregorio Borgia / AP by Mike Newall Published Oct. 11, 2026, 11:45 a.m. ET Listen to article • 0:00 min Pope Leo XIV said he would undergo surgery in the coming days so doctors can remove a small growth discovered in his lung. The procedure marks his first major medical issue since becoming the first U.S.-born pontiff last year. Speaking during his regular Sunday address in St. Peter’s Square, the 71-year-old said doctors had detected the nodule “at a very early stage” and that it was “well localized.” He decided to follow doctors’ recommendations to have it removed. The surgery is expected to take place at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital. The pope is expected to require some hospitalization during his weeklong recovery, Vatican officials said. “Thank you for your spiritual closeness, and I entrust myself to your prayers,” Leo told worshipers. It is unclear if Pope Leo will still be able to present Villanova University’s inaugural sustainability medal in his name at an international conference in Rome on Tuesday. A Villanova alumnus, Pope Leo is scheduled to bestow the award to Cardinal Michael Czerny, who founded an AIDS network. Nodules are small, often non-symptomatic, lung lesions that prove cancerous in less than 5% of patients, according to the American Cancer Society . They are often discovered during unrelated screenings. Procedures to remove them are considered routine. The Vatican did not release any further details about the nodule. Pope Leo XIV is not known to suffer from any serious medical ailments. The physically active pontiff maintains a home gym in his newly renovated papal apartment. The operation is not expected to affect the pope’s trip to Latin America in November, Vatican officials said. The Pope Leo XIV Sustainability Medal was established earlier this year, inspired in part by Pope Leo’s call to serve the poor and vulnerable, Villanova officials said. “Care for creation cannot be separated from care for people,” the school said. Czerny, who was born in Czechoslovakia and raised and ordained in Canada, has focused on helping vulnerable people worldwide for decades.
